 East Africa faces uneven rains as El Niño raises flood threat -report
 Sunday 15th November, 2026 02:20 PM | 
 By Aloys Michael 
 Heavy rainfall has caused flooding in parts of Tana River County.PHOTO/@KenyaRedCross/X 
 East Africa is heading into a critical phase of its October–December rainy season, with strengthening El Niño conditions expected to bring above-average rainfall but increasing the threat of flooding, crop losses and disruptions to agricultural activities across the region .
 A new assessment by the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) warns that the rainfall season has started unevenly, with Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi experiencing relatively dry conditions in September and October despite forecasts of above-average precipitation.
 The November 13 report says the combination of a strengthening El Niño and a positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) is likely to enhance cumulative rainfall across much of East Africa, with November expected to be the peak rainfall month.
 However, the anticipated increase in rainfall comes after months of poor precipitation that have already affected agricultural production in several countries, raising concerns about the region’s ability to recover without suffering further weather-related damage.
 FEWS NET warns that the distribution of rainfall remains uncertain, meaning some areas could benefit from improved agricultural conditions while others face intense downpours and flooding.
 People Daily digital screengrab of the FEWS NET weather forecast 
 Poor rainfall leaves agricultural production under pressure 
 The changing weather outlook follows a difficult June–September season, when prolonged dry spells and above-average temperatures affected major agricultural production zones across East Africa.
 FEWS NET estimates that rainfall during the period was generally between 45 and 90 per cent of the long-term average across regions experiencing their respective rainy seasons.
 In Kenya, Trans Nzoia, Uasin Gishu and Nakuru experienced substantial rainfall deficits during critical crop-growing stages. Preliminary assessments indicate national maize yield deficits of approximately 28 per cent, with losses reaching 43 per cent in high-potential production counties.
 Uganda also experienced dry and hot conditions between April and August, affecting sorghum production, particularly in agricultural areas of Karamoja.
 In South Sudan, persistent rainfall deficits affected agricultural zones in Jonglei, Upper Nile and Unity, while poor Kiremt rainfall in Ethiopia undermined the Meher production season in parts of Tigray, eastern Amhara, Afar and eastern Oromia.
 The report says the late-season improvement in rainfall was insufficient to reverse the accumulated moisture deficits.
 Nearly 874,000 people in Somalia could be displaced by flooding between October and December.PHOTO/@IOM_EHSA/X 
 “Although some improvement in rainfall was observed towards the end of the season, particularly in parts of central and western Ethiopia, the late-season rains were insufficient to reverse the accumulated deficits,” FEWS NET states.
 The situation has also affected the current planting season. Parts of Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi received isolated rainfall that triggered planting, but the precipitation was insufficient to sustain favourable crop germination.
 In western and coastal Kenya, false rainfall starts were followed by dry spells, creating the likelihood of replanting in affected areas.
 The anticipated establishment of seasonal rainfall could therefore provide an important opportunity for agricultural recovery, although the timing and distribution of the rains will remain critical.
 Rising river levels signal growing flood risks 
 While improved rainfall could help restore soil moisture and support crop development, the beginning of the October–December season has already brought flooding in parts of the region .
 FEWS NET reports above-average rainfall across much of southern and central Somalia, southern and eastern Ethiopia, and localised parts of eastern Kenya.
 The heavy precipitation has triggered localised flooding and rapidly rising river levels, particularly within Somalia’s Juba and Shabelle river catchments.
 At Jowhar in Somalia, the Shabelle River rose from 2.48 metres on September 29 to 5.38 metres by the week ending October 14, approaching its bankfull level of 5.5 metres.
 People Daily digital screengrab of the FEWS NET weather forecast 
 In Kenya, seasonal rivers in Moyale reached bankfull levels within 24 hours after estimated rainfall of 133 millimetres on October 28. Tana River County also experienced localised flooding during the same week.
 The developments highlight the potential consequences of intense rainfall in areas exposed to river flooding, particularly as forecasts point to increased precipitation in November and December.
 “Flood risk remains high for the remainder of the season across East Africa particularly within flood prone areas,” the report warns.
 The agency further cautions that episodes of intense rainfall could increase the risks of riverine flooding, flash floods and waterlogging, potentially disrupting agricultural activities.
 However, the flood threat is not uniform across the region. The report identifies specific locations where heavy rainfall and rising river levels have already been observed, while warning that the distribution of future rainfall remains uncertain.
 Floods carried away livestock in Tana River.PHOTO/screngrab by People Daily Digital/Local station 
 El Niño could influence rainfall beyond December 
 FEWS NET attributes the expected increase in rainfall partly to strengthening El Niño conditions combined with the positive Indian Ocean Dipole.
 The two climate phenomena are expected to enhance cumulative October–December rainfall across much of East Africa, with forecasts indicating that rainfall will intensify from November onwards.
 The areas expected to receive increased rainfall include much of Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi, as well as central Ethiopia, southern Somalia and southern South Sudan.
 The anticipated precipitation could improve crop development in areas where planting has already taken place and support the recovery of pasture and surface water resources following prolonged dry conditions.
 Pastoral areas have begun experiencing some recovery, although FEWS NET says improvements remain uneven, with pasture regeneration and water availability still limited in several locations.
 The agency expects the Indian Ocean Dipole to weaken slightly but remain positive, while El Niño is forecast to strengthen further, reaching its peak around December 2026.
 “Current climate outlooks indicate a high likelihood of El Niño conditions persisting into early 2027,” the report states.
 The persistence of the climate phenomenon could prolong its influence on regional rainfall patterns beyond the current rainy season.
 For governments across East Africa, the outlook presents competing priorities: supporting agricultural recovery after months of rainfall deficits while strengthening preparedness against flooding and other weather-related disruptions.
 The report’s findings underscore the importance of monitoring rainfall distribution, river levels and ground conditions as the season progresses, particularly in areas already experiencing flooding.
